concept.title: Router Placement
concept.shortdesc: The location of the router affects Wi-Fi coverage, signal strength, and network performance. Place the router in a central and open location to provide reliable wireless coverage.

section.title: Overview
section.p: The sends Wi-Fi signals to wireless devices within its coverage area. Walls, floors, furniture, appliances, and other wireless devices can reduce the signal strength.
Place the near the center of the required coverage area. An open and elevated location usually provides better coverage than a low or enclosed location.
section.note: Put the router where the signal has a clear path to frequently used wireless devices.
Evaluate signal strength and channel usage at different locations before you select the final router location.

section.title: Recommended Location
section.p: Select a location that meets the following conditions:

ul.li: The location is near the center of the required coverage area.
The router is on a stable and elevated surface.
The router is in an open area.
Air can move freely around the router.
The location is near an electrical outlet.
The location permits a wired connection to the or Optical Network Terminal (ONT).
The router is away from large metal objects and sources of wireless interference.

section.note: Keep the ventilation openings on the clear. Restricted airflow can cause the router to become too hot.

section.title: Locations to Avoid
section.p: Do not put the in the following locations:

ul.li: Inside a closed cabinet or drawer
Behind a television or large appliance
Near a cordless telephone base station
Near mirrors or large glass surfaces
Near thick concrete or brick walls
Near heat sources or direct sunlight
Near water or areas with high moisture

section.note: Do not put the router near water, excessive heat, or a location where the router can fall.

section.title: Router Height
section.p: Put the on a shelf, desk, or other stable surface above floor level. Do not put the router directly on the floor.
An elevated position can reduce obstructions between the router and wireless devices.
section.note: Make sure that the router and its cables do not create a trip hazard.

section.title: Antenna Orientation
section.p: If the has adjustable antennas, position the antennas as specified in the installation instructions.
Different antenna positions can provide wireless coverage in different directions. Test the Wi-Fi signal after you change an antenna position.
section.note: Do not force an antenna beyond its permitted movement range. This action can damage the antenna or its connector.
Change the orientation of the only when coverage measurements show that a different orientation improves the required coverage area.

section.title: Placement in a Multistory Home
section.p: In a multistory home, place the near the center of the home and between the floors that require Wi-Fi coverage.
Floors and ceilings can reduce the Wi-Fi signal. Test the connection on each floor after you select the router location.
If one router does not provide sufficient coverage, use the or to extend the wireless network.

section.title: Reduce Wireless Interference
section.p: Keep the away from devices that use radio signals in the same frequency range.
Potential sources of interference include microwave ovens, cordless telephones, wireless cameras, Bluetooth devices, and nearby Wi-Fi networks.
section.note: If the Wi-Fi connection becomes slow or unstable near an appliance, move the router or the wireless device away from the appliance.
Review channel utilization and neighboring wireless networks before you manually select a channel. Use automatic channel selection when interference conditions change frequently.

section.title: Evaluate the Router Location
section.p: Test the Wi-Fi connection in the rooms where users frequently connect wireless devices.
Check the signal strength, connection stability, and network performance at each location. Move the router if the signal is weak in an important coverage area.
section.note: Test the network with a smartphone, laptop, or tablet. Confirm that the device remains connected as you move through the required coverage area.
Record signal strength, channel utilization, and throughput at selected test locations. Compare the results before and after you move the router.

section.title: When to Extend Wi-Fi Coverage
section.p: Router placement cannot remove all coverage problems. Large homes, multistory homes, and buildings with dense construction can require additional wireless equipment.
Use the when a wired Ethernet connection is available in the area that requires more coverage. Use the when multiple wireless coverage points are required.
section.note: Do not put an access point or mesh node in an area that has no usable connection to the main router. Put the device between the router and the area with a weak signal.
Use a wired backhaul connection when possible. A wired backhaul can provide more consistent performance than a shared wireless backhaul.
